posts.title: DisAble Advocacy (article) (part 1) by Leanne Dyck
posts.description: The history of disabled advocacy in Canada. This article is constructed from quotations. I would like to thank the authors of these articles for their fine work. I list the sources at the end of "DisAbled Advocacy: Sharing Our Truth."--which I will publish next Sunday. photo by ldyck DisAbled Advocacy: Sharing Our Truth Disabled rights activism in Canada refers to the social and political movements aimed at advocating for the rights of people with disabilities. Disability rights activists and allies have, since the mid-twentieth century, been fighting for the rights of more than 6.2 million Canadians with one or more disabilities to be treated as full and equal citizens. [1] Widespread trust in medical authority and the growth of industrialization created a set of social, political and economic conditions during the 19 th and early 20 th centuries that fostered the segregation of disabled people in Canada. posts.title: Book Review: All the Light We Cannot See by Anthony Doerr (historical fiction)
posts.description: All The Light You Cannot See, set during the Second World War, is about a short boy with a huge heart who tried to do what he thought was right and a blind girl full of courage who did what she could. All the Light You Cannot See addresses two stereotypes: that all Germans living in Germany during the Second World War were evil and that all people living in occupied countries during the war were weak. All The Light You Cannot See is written in short chapters—which made this tomb of over 500 pages accessible for this dyslexic. The chapters are full of beauty and brutality. I'm sure this book will continue to haunt me long after I've savoured the final chapter. Favourite quote... "a voice on the radio offering a loom on which to spin his dreams." After reading and watching the Netflix series, I highly recommend both. In fact, I think watching the TV adaptation helps me live with some aspects of the book.
